questions.q: Why is a schema change on a source table dangerous for an incremental model specifically?
options: It only affects seeds, never models
It has no effect at all on incremental models
Rows built before the change never re-run against the new column, so it's null for old rows and populated only going forward — invisible until someone notices
It causes the entire dbt project to fail to compile immediately
questions.explain: Because an incremental model never reprocesses old rows, a new or changed source column is silently missing from historical rows, which looks like a data quality bug rather than a schema issue.

questions.q: How can late-arriving data get permanently missed by an incremental model?
options: Late-arriving data is always automatically included by dbt regardless of timestamp
dbt automatically detects and re-includes late rows without any config
It causes the model to throw a compile error
If a row arrives after the watermark has already advanced past its timestamp, the is_incremental() filter excludes it and it's never picked up again
questions.explain: The filter trusts the timestamp reflects arrival time; a row that arrives late with an old timestamp falls behind an already-advanced watermark and gets silently skipped.

options: Only refreshes the dbt docs site, not any data
Drops the model's target table and rebuilds it from scratch, ignoring is_incremental() filtering entirely
Re-runs only the single most recent row
Deletes the model definition from the project
questions.explain: --full-refresh rebuilds the table from the same SELECT that runs on a brand-new model's first build, so nothing gets filtered out — fixing both schema drift and missed late arrivals.

questions.q: What is a 'lookback window,' and what does it trade off?
options: A type of snapshot strategy
Re-checking a few recent periods every run to catch late arrivals, at the cost of some redundant reprocessing
A dbt Cloud feature for viewing historical job logs
A setting that disables incremental models entirely
questions.explain: A lookback window widens the incremental filter to re-check a few recent days, trading a little redundant work for catching rows that arrived late.

questions.q: Why shouldn't `--full-refresh` be run casually on every deploy?
options: It is not a real dbt command and doesn't exist
It permanently deletes the model's source data
It has zero cost, so there's no reason not to — the lesson just avoids recommending it
It costs exactly what the incremental model was built to avoid — a full reprocessing of the entire history
questions.explain: A full refresh reprocesses everything, which is the exact cost incremental models exist to avoid — the healthy pattern is scheduling it periodically, not running it on every deploy.
